# SK2211 — Nothing the loop condition reads is changed by the loop

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

Every local and parameter the loop condition reads keeps its value for the whole loop, and nothing in the body can leave it, so the loop either never runs or never stops.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `LoopVariableIsNeverChangedInsideLoop` (`resharper_loop_variable_is_never_changed_inside_loop_highlighting`) |

## Why

⚠ **An infinite loop is usually the point, so "the loop has no exit" is the wrong question to ask.** `while (true)` is the event loop, the reactor and the retry pump, and a rule that reported it would be reporting the shape every server is built out of. The narrower and answerable question is whether the condition can ever come out differently: a loop whose condition reads only locals and parameters, none of which the body writes, evaluates the same expression to the same value on every pass. Combined with a body that cannot `break`, `return` or `throw` its way out, the loop is decided before it starts — it runs zero times or it hangs — and the increment that was meant to be there is missing. That is a defect no `while (true)` is, and it is provable from definite-assignment alone, with no value reasoning and no lattice.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var i = 0;
while (i < count) {
    Sum(i);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
var i = 0;
while (i < count) {
    Sum(i);
    i++;
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A condition that reads anything but a local or a parameter is declined, and that exclusion is the rule's whole false-positive story.** `while (!stopped)` on a field, `while (queue.Count > 0)`, `while (reader.Read())` and `while (token.IsCancellationRequested)` all read state some other statement, some other thread or some other object changes, and none of them is decidable here; only locals and parameters have a single writer this analysis can enumerate. A method call, a property, an element access, `this`, a field and an `await` anywhere in the condition each withdraw the finding. ⚠ **So does an increment, a decrement or an assignment in the condition itself, and that guard was missing until the corpus found it.** Newtonsoft's `while (digits-- != 0)` writes `digits` in the condition, so the body has no reason to — and the rule reported a loop that terminates perfectly well. `AnalyzeDataFlow` is asked about the *body* and answers correctly; the question was the incomplete half. ⚠ **A constant condition is not reported.** `while (true)` and `for (;;)` are the idiom, and the rule is deliberately silent on them — the finding is a condition that *could* have changed and does not, not one that was never going to. ⚠ **The body is checked for an exit and the check over-bails.** Any `return`, `throw`, `break`, `goto` or `yield break` anywhere in the body withdraws the finding, whether or not it is reachable, because a rule that told somebody their loop hangs when a `return` two branches down ends it is a wrong finding rather than a noisy one. A `for` loop with any incrementor is declined for the same reason. ⚠ **A condition variable that any lambda or local function in the member so much as mentions withdraws the finding**, because a delegate created before the loop and invoked inside it writes through the closure without the write appearing in the body's data flow. A `ref` local is declined: its value can change through the alias. Writes made by passing a variable as a `ref` or `out` argument inside the body are counted as writes, so the loop that hands its counter to a helper is not reported. Generated code is excluded.
